content: In the field of medicine, certain blood tests are performed using venous blood obtained through a fingerprick. This involves creating a small puncture wound that yields only a few drops of blood. While the procedure can be painful, it is often quicker and less distressing than venipuncture. Once a droplet of blood forms, it is typically collected using a capillary tube, which is a thin glass tube. The blood is usually drawn passively or, in some cases, through indirect suction. Common tests conducted on capillary blood include glucose level measurements. Diabetic patients frequently use portable blood glucose meters to monitor their blood sugar levels. Another common test is the measurement of hemoglobin levels. Fingerprick testing for hemoglobin is a rapid screening method used to determine if a blood donor has a sufficient blood count to be eligible for donation. Fingerprick procedures are sometimes performed on children and elderly individuals when only a small volume of blood, typically less than 500 micrograms, is required for testing. In neonates (newborn babies), heel pricks are preferred over fingerpricks. This approach minimizes the risk of permanent damage and is more suitable due to the small size of a newborn’s fingers.
